name: Choice-Supportive Bias
description: People remember a past choice as better than it really was, attributing more positives to what they chose and more negatives to what they rejected. Memory becomes a quiet advocate for the committed option.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to retrospective feedback, satisfaction surveys, post-choice evaluations, vendor/tool selection debriefs, and any research that asks people to remember why they chose one product over another.
prevalence_note: Known in decision and memory research, but the exact label is uncommon in mainstream product-design vocabulary outside specialist research-methods discussions.

findings.description: Reviewing the choice-supportive misremembering literature, Lind et al. concluded that empirical support is solid mainly for misattribution in recognition-memory tasks, but substantially weaker for fact distortion, false memory, and selective forgetting.
findings.source_title: Choice-Supportive Misremembering: A New Taxonomy and Review

findings.description: When remembering past decisions, participants made source-monitoring errors that favored their chosen option: they attributed more positive features to the selected option and more negative features to the rejected one, both correctly and incorrectly.
findings.source_title: Misremembrance of Options Past: Source Monitoring and Choice
